subject: physics
title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
welcome_lead: Integrate Q V to find the energy locked in a charged capacitor.
meta_desc: A-Level Capacitance adventure on energy stored as ½CV² and ½QV.
final_note: Half the work goes to the capacitor, half to resistive losses when charging from a battery.

concepts.def: Same energy, using C and V.
Same energy, using Q and C.
Area under Q vs V triangle.
50% of battery energy wasted in charging R.

walkthroughs.body_html: As charge builds, voltage rises linearly from 0 to V. Total energy is the area under the line, which is ½ × Q × V — a triangle.
E = ½ Q V = ½ C V² = Q² / (2C). Use whichever pair you know. Doubling V quadruples stored energy.
Battery delivers QV of energy when charging. Half ends up as ½ Q V on the capacitor; the other half is dissipated in resistance, regardless of R value.

mcqs.q: When energy is 'lost' as heat due to friction, what has really happened?
options: Energy has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings — it's not destroyed, just dissipated.
Energy has been used up and no longer exists.
Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.

mcqs.q: If a car doubles its speed, what happens to its kinetic energy?
options: Kinetic energy doubles because energy is proportional to speed.
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
It quadruples (because KE = 1/2 mv^2 — kinetic energy is proportional to v^2).

mcqs.q: Is the internal energy of a system the same as the heat it contains?
options: No — a system doesn't 'contain heat'; internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles, changed by heating or doing work.
Yes — internal energy is just the stored heat in the object.
Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
